d: The stage depicts the interior of the church of the Katharinen in an oblique average. From the main nave, which can be extended to itself from the background to the left, only the last rows of the church chairs are visible. The foreground is occupied by the free space in front of the choir; this is later closed too completely by a black curtain against the ship. In the last row of the church chairs are Eve and Magdalene; Walther von Stolzing, at some distance, is leaning to the side of a pillar, clinginging to the eyes of Eve, who repeatedly turns to him with a silent play of gestures.
There are still several teaching boys; they carry and make benches and direct everything to the meeting of the Meistersinger

At the end of the benches, in the middle of the stage, there is the "memorial" scaffold, which was previously erected. To the left is the raised, catheder-like chair (the "singing chair") facing the assembly. In the background, along the big curtain, stands a long lower bench for the apprentices. Walther, sadly above the ridicule of the boys, has settled on the front bench. Pogner and Beckmesser have appeared in the conversation from the sacristy. The teaching boys are waiting, reverently standing in front of the back bench. Only David initially stands up at the entrance of the sacristy.

The stage represents in the foreground a road in the length average, which is cut in the middle by a narrow alley, turning to the background too crooked, so that in front two corner houses appear, one of which is richer - to the right - the house of Pogners, the other simpler - to the left - that of Hans Sachs. - In front of Pogner's house a linden tree; in front of Saxony a lilac tree. Cheerful summer evening, in the course of the first appearances gradually breaking in. David is about to close the shutters after the alley from outside.
Pogener and Eve, returning home from the walk, slightly hung the daughter by the father's arms, quietly came up the alley
Sachs has returned from the inside to the workshop in light house clothes. He turns to David, who has remained at his work table
Eva stepped on the street, shyly approached the workshop and now stands unnoticed at the door at Sachs
Walther has come up the alley; now he bends around the corner: Eve sees him, rips away from Magdalene and throws Walther into the street
Beckmesser, following the night watchman, has come up the alley, peeked at the windows of Pogener's house and, leaning on Saxony's house, he now agrees with his lute brought with him.

In Sachs' workshop. Short space. In the background the half-opened shop door, leading to the street. On the right side a chamber door. On the left side the window, with flower sticks in front of it, a work table. Sachs sits on a large armchair at this window, through which the morning sun shines brightly on him: He has a large foliant in front of him on the shot and is deepened in reading. David, coming from the street, under the shop door, is lying in, and as he sees Sachs, he returns. However, he assures himself that Sachs does not notice him, slips in, puts his basket on the back counter at the shop and examines his content: He fetches flowers and ribbons and crawls them on the table, at last he finds on the bottom a sausage and a cake and at once lets himself be consumed as Sachs, who constantly does not pay attention to him, with a strong sound of one of the large leaves of the foliage turning around.
Walther enters under the chamber door. He stops there for a moment and looks at Sachs. He turns and lets the folian glide to the ground.

Beckmesser. Sachs. Beckmesser, which appears outside the shop, is in great excitement and, as he finds the workshop empty, hastily enters. He is richly cleaned up, but in a very suffering condition. He looks around under the door again exactly in the workshop, then he limps forwards, but twitches together and cuts his back. He again takes some steps, but pinches his knees and now cuts them. He sits on the shoe-stool, but quickly starts painfully again. He looks at the stool and gets into more and more excited meditation. He is tormented by the most painful memories and ideas; he starts to snatch the sweat from his forehead more and more unquietly. He limps around and stares at himself more and more vividly. As if he were persecuted from all sides, he tammers back and forth.
Eve, richly decorated, in shiny white clothes, a little suffering and pale, steps in to the shop and slowly moves forward

The curtains have been raised to the height; the stage has been transformed. This presents a free meadow plan, in the wider background the city of Nuremberg. The Pegnitz winds through the plan, the narrow river is kept practicable at the next points. Colour-flagged barges set the arriving, festively dressed citizens of the guilds with women and children, on the banks of the meadow. An elevated stage with benches and seats on it is mounted to the right; it is already decorated with the flags of the arrived guilds; in the course the flag bearers of the still arriving guilds also place their flags around the singer stage so that it is finally completely enclosed to three sides. Tents with drinks and refreshments of all kinds limit the sides of the front main room by the rest. In front of the tents it is already funny: citizens sit with women, children and journeymen sit and store there. The teacher's cabs, firmly dressed, rich and gracefully decorated with flowers and ribbons, practice with slender stems, which are also decorated with floral ladies and journeymen.
